question: A nurse on the ward is preparing medicines for intravenous use for a client. Which practice BEST prevents the spread of infection?
option_1: Use the same needle for several vials of the drug
option_2: Clean the hands and use a sterile technique for every preparation
option_3: Prepare the doses in advance in one syringe
option_4: Recap the needle with both hands after the injection
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Clean the hands and use a sterile technique for every preparation

Clinical Rationale: Hand hygiene with a strict sterile technique for every preparation is the MOST effective way to prevent infection during intravenous medicine preparation.

Key Clue: preventing infection while preparing medicines for intravenous use on the ward

Priority Principle: Infection control

Why Not Others: (a) Reusing a needle contaminates the vials and spreads organisms; (c) Preparing doses in advance allows organisms to grow in the syringe; (d) Recapping with both hands invites a needle stick injury.

PGI Exam Trap: The same needle is used for several vials.

5-Second Recall: Clean the hands and use a sterile technique for every preparation.

PNC Exam Pearl: Prepare each dose at the time it is due.

question: A 70-year-old man on the ward is prescribed a drug by a verbal order. Which pair of drug names is the MOST likely to be confused with each other?
option_1: Hydralazine and hydroxyzine
option_2: Aspirin and clopidogrel
option_3: Metformin and glibenclamide
option_4: Furosemide and spironolactone
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Hydralazine and hydroxyzine

Clinical Rationale: Hydralazine and hydroxyzine sound and look alike, so they are a well known look alike and sound alike pair that can be confused in orders.

Key Clue: pair of drug names easily confused during a verbal order on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (b) Aspirin and clopidogrel are different in sound and spelling; (c) Metformin and glibenclamide are not easily confused in speech; (d) Furosemide and spironolactone look and sound quite different.

PGI Exam Trap: Look alike names are treated as if they were clearly different.

5-Second Recall: Write down and read back verbal orders for look alike drugs.

PNC Exam Pearl: Tall man lettering helps to separate similar drug names.

question: A 50-year-old woman on the ward is prescribed a subcutaneous injection. Which technique is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to use?
option_1: Give the injection into a hard scarred area
option_2: Insert the needle at 10 degrees into the skin
option_3: Insert the needle at 90 degrees into the muscle
option_4: Insert the needle into the fatty tissue at 45 to 90 degrees
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Insert the needle into the fatty tissue at 45 to 90 degrees

Clinical Rationale: Subcutaneous tissue lies under the skin, so the needle is inserted at 45 to 90 degrees into the fatty layer where the drug is absorbed slowly.

Key Clue: technique of a subcutaneous injection in a woman on the ward

Priority Principle: Skill / Medication

Why Not Others: (a) Hard scarred tissue absorbs the drug poorly; (b) A 10 degree angle places the drug just under the skin, which is intradermal; (c) A 90 degree angle into muscle is an intramuscular injection.

PGI Exam Trap: The angle for a subcutaneous injection is confused with other routes.

5-Second Recall: Subcutaneous injections go into the fatty layer at 45 to 90 degrees.

PNC Exam Pearl: Rotate the sites to prevent hard lumps forming.

question: A 65-year-old man on the ward who takes warfarin is prescribed a course of an antibiotic. Which advice is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Stop the warfarin while the antibiotic is being taken
option_2: Double the warfarin dose if the infection is severe
option_3: Report any unusual bleeding or bruising to the doctor at once
option_4: Take both medicines together on an empty stomach
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Report any unusual bleeding or bruising to the doctor at once

Clinical Rationale: Many antibiotics raise the effect of warfarin and increase the bleeding risk, so the client must report any unusual bleeding or bruising at once.

Key Clue: client on warfarin who is prescribed an antibiotic on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug interaction

Why Not Others: (a) Stopping warfarin without advice risks a clot; (b) Doubling the warfarin without an order can cause severe bleeding; (d) Taking the two together does not remove the interaction.

PGI Exam Trap: The raised bleeding risk of the combination is NOT mentioned.

5-Second Recall: Antibiotics can increase the effect of warfarin.

PNC Exam Pearl: Check the international normalised ratio more often during such a course.

Reference Table: Therapeutic drug levels & monitoring - Digoxin: 0.5-2.0 ng/mL (toxic > 2.0); Lithium: 0.6-1.2 mEq/L (toxic > 1.5); Phenytoin: 10-20 mcg/mL; INR (warfarin): Therapeutic 2-3; aPTT (heparin): 1.5-2.5 x control.

question: A 35-year-old man who comes to the clinic with a cough is taking treatment for tuberculosis and develops yellow eyes with nausea. Which action is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to take?
option_1: Double the dose so that the course is finished faster
option_2: Continue the same dose and review the client after a month
option_3: Stop the drug and refer the client for assessment at once
option_4: Change to a herbal remedy for the stomach upset
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Stop the drug and refer the client for assessment at once

Clinical Rationale: Yellow eyes with nausea on antitubercular treatment suggests drug induced liver injury, so the drug is stopped and the client referred at once.

Key Clue: yellow eyes with nausea during treatment for tuberculosis in a man at the clinic

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) A higher dose increases the liver damage; (b) Continuing the drug allows the liver injury to worsen; (d) A herbal remedy does not treat drug induced hepatitis.

PGI Exam Trap: A sign of liver injury is watched until the next review.

5-Second Recall: Yellow eyes on antitubercular treatment means liver injury.

PNC Exam Pearl: Warn every client about the warning signs of liver injury.

question: A nurse on the ward has just given a client the wrong dose of a medicine. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Wait to see whether the client has any effect
option_2: Record the incident and tell the client later
option_3: Give the correct dose straight away
option_4: Assess the client and inform the doctor at once
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Assess the client and inform the doctor at once

Clinical Rationale: The client is the FIRST concern, so the nurse assesses the client for harm and informs the doctor at once, then records the incident.

Key Clue: wrong dose of a medicine has been given to a client on the ward

Priority Principle: Safety / Medication

Why Not Others: (a) Waiting allows harm to go unnoticed and untreated; (b) Telling the client later delays both assessment and treatment; (c) Giving the correct dose before assessment may add to the overdose.

PGI Exam Trap: The incident report is written before the client is assessed.

5-Second Recall: Assess the client first and inform the doctor after a medication error.

PNC Exam Pearl: Record the error honestly after the client is safe.

question: A 4-year-old child on the ward has a swollen and pale site around an intravenous cannula. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Stop the infusion and remove the cannula
option_2: Increase the rate to keep the vein open
option_3: Massage the site to disperse the fluid
option_4: Apply heat and continue the infusion
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Stop the infusion and remove the cannula

Clinical Rationale: Swelling and pallor around the cannula mean the fluid is going into the tissues, so the infusion is stopped and the cannula removed at once.

Key Clue: swollen and pale site around a child's intravenous cannula on the ward

Priority Principle: Safety / Device

Why Not Others: (b) A faster rate pushes more fluid into the tissues; (c) Massaging spreads the fluid and may cause tissue damage; (d) Heat and continuing the infusion worsen the extravasation.

PGI Exam Trap: The infusion is continued when the fluid is in the tissues.

5-Second Recall: Stop the infusion at once in a suspected extravasation.

PNC Exam Pearl: Raise the limb and apply the prescribed compress after removing the cannula.

question: A 70-year-old woman on the ward who takes digoxin has a serum potassium of 3.0 mEq/L. Which statement about the risk of digoxin toxicity is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: A low potassium level protects against digoxin toxicity
option_2: A low potassium level increases the risk of digoxin toxicity
option_3: Digoxin itself raises the serum potassium level
option_4: Potassium has no effect on the action of digoxin
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) A low potassium level increases the risk of digoxin toxicity

Clinical Rationale: Digoxin and potassium compete at the heart muscle, so a low potassium level makes the heart more sensitive to digoxin and raises the risk of toxicity.

Key Clue: serum potassium of 3.0 mEq/L in a woman on digoxin on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) A low potassium increases rather than reduces the toxicity risk; (c) Digoxin does not raise the serum potassium level; (d) Potassium strongly affects the action of digoxin.

PGI Exam Trap: A low potassium is thought to be protective in clients on digoxin.

5-Second Recall: Hypokalaemia increases digoxin toxicity.

PNC Exam Pearl: Diuretics that lower potassium are watched closely with digoxin.

Reference Table: Normal serum electrolyte ranges - Sodium (Na+): 135-145 mEq/L; Potassium (K+): 3.5-5.0 mEq/L; Chloride (Cl-): 98-106 mEq/L; Calcium (total): 8.5-10.5 mg/dL; Magnesium (Mg2+): 1.5-2.5 mEq/L; Phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL.

question: A 30-year-old woman who comes to the clinic is prescribed oral tetracycline. Which instruction is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Take it with an antacid to control the heartburn
option_2: Take it with a glass of milk to reduce stomach upset
option_3: Avoid taking it with milk, antacids or iron preparations
option_4: Take it at bedtime together with an iron tablet
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Avoid taking it with milk, antacids or iron preparations

Clinical Rationale: Milk, antacids and iron bind tetracycline in the gut and stop it being absorbed, so they are avoided around the dose.

Key Clue: client prescribed oral tetracycline at the clinic

Priority Principle: Drug interaction

Why Not Others: (a) Antacids bind the drug and reduce absorption; (b) Milk reduces the absorption of tetracycline; (d) Iron binds tetracycline and reduces its effect.

PGI Exam Trap: The drug is taken with the very substances that bind it.

5-Second Recall: Tetracycline is taken on an empty stomach away from milk and antacids.

PNC Exam Pearl: Tetracycline can stain the teeth of young children.

question: A 40-year-old man on the ward needs an intramuscular injection. Which site is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to choose to reduce the risk of nerve injury?
option_1: The lower inner part of the buttock
option_2: The front of the mid thigh
option_3: The inner upper arm
option_4: The ventrogluteal site on the hip
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) The ventrogluteal site on the hip

Clinical Rationale: The ventrogluteal site on the hip is free of large nerves and blood vessels and is the safest site for an intramuscular injection.

Key Clue: safest site for an intramuscular injection in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Clinical anatomy

Why Not Others: (a) The buttock has a large nerve in its lower inner part; (b) The front of the thigh is used in infants and has less muscle bulk in adults; (c) The inner upper arm contains nerves and vessels close to the surface.

PGI Exam Trap: A site close to a large nerve is chosen.

5-Second Recall: The ventrogluteal site is the safest for intramuscular injection.

PNC Exam Pearl: Landmarks are used rather than guessing the site.

question: A 20-year-old man on the ward is about to receive his medicine. Which statement about the rights of medication administration is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: The nurse checks the right client, drug, dose, route and time before giving any medicine
option_2: The dose may be reduced if the client looks unwell
option_3: The time of administration may be changed by several hours without an order
option_4: The route may be changed by the nurse to suit the client
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) The nurse checks the right client, drug, dose, route and time before giving any medicine

Clinical Rationale: The nurse checks the right client, drug, dose, route and time before every dose, because each of these can cause harm if it is wrong.

Key Clue: rights of medication administration for a client on the ward

Priority Principle: Safety / Medication

Why Not Others: (b) Only the prescriber can change a dose; (c) Timing is not altered without a prescriber's order; (d) The route is changed only by the prescriber.

PGI Exam Trap: The nurse changes the dose or route to suit the client.

5-Second Recall: Check client, drug, dose, route and time before every dose.

PNC Exam Pearl: Document the dose immediately after it is given.

question: A 45-year-old man on the ward develops a widespread rash with wheezing minutes after the FIRST dose of an antibiotic. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Give the next dose as ordered
option_2: Stop the drug and inform the doctor at once
option_3: Apply a soothing lotion to the rash
option_4: Slow the infusion and continue with it
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Stop the drug and inform the doctor at once

Clinical Rationale: A rash with wheezing minutes after a FIRST dose suggests a drug allergy, so the drug is stopped and the doctor informed at once.

Key Clue: widespread rash with wheezing minutes after a FIRST dose of an antibiotic

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Another dose may cause a severe reaction; (c) A lotion does not treat the general reaction; (d) Continuing the infusion allows the reaction to worsen.

PGI Exam Trap: A general reaction is treated as a local skin problem.

5-Second Recall: Stop the drug at once in a suspected drug allergy.

PNC Exam Pearl: Record the allergy clearly and tell the client about it.

question: A 60-year-old woman on the ward refuses a prescribed medicine. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Mix the medicine into the food without telling the client
option_2: Force the client to take the medicine
option_3: Ask the client the reason and inform the doctor
option_4: Record it as given so that the chart stays complete
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Ask the client the reason and inform the doctor

Clinical Rationale: A client has the right to refuse, so the nurse finds out why and informs the doctor so that the plan can be reviewed.

Key Clue: client refuses a prescribed medicine on the ward

Priority Principle: Ethics / Medication

Why Not Others: (a) Hiding a drug in food is dishonest and unsafe; (b) Forcing a medicine takes away the client's right to refuse; (d) Falsely recording the drug as given is a serious error.

PGI Exam Trap: The refusal is recorded as if the medicine had been given.

5-Second Recall: Respect the client's refusal and inform the doctor.

PNC Exam Pearl: Record the refusal with the reason in the notes.

question: A 70-year-old woman on the ward who takes a diuretic has a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. Which action is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to anticipate?
option_1: An increase in the dose of the same diuretic
option_2: A change in the diuretic or the addition of a potassium supplement
option_3: A potassium restricted diet
option_4: No action because the value is within the normal range
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) A change in the diuretic or the addition of a potassium supplement

Clinical Rationale: A potassium of 3.1 is low and is often caused by loop or thiazide diuretics, so the drug may be changed or a supplement added.

Key Clue: serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L in a woman on a diuretic on the ward

Priority Principle: Lab interpretation

Why Not Others: (a) A higher dose of the same diuretic lowers the potassium further; (c) A potassium restricted diet would make the deficit worse; (d) The value is below the normal range and needs action.

PGI Exam Trap: A low potassium caused by diuretics is left untreated.

5-Second Recall: Thiazide and loop diuretics lower the serum potassium.

PNC Exam Pearl: Encourage foods rich in potassium while on these drugs.

Reference Table: Normal serum electrolyte ranges - Sodium (Na+): 135-145 mEq/L; Potassium (K+): 3.5-5.0 mEq/L; Chloride (Cl-): 98-106 mEq/L; Calcium (total): 8.5-10.5 mg/dL; Magnesium (Mg2+): 1.5-2.5 mEq/L; Phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL.

question: A 55-year-old man on the ward is prescribed a high alert drug. Which medicine is the MOST likely to be this drug?
option_1: Insulin
option_2: Paracetamol
option_3: Oral iron
option_4: Vitamin C
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Insulin

Clinical Rationale: Insulin is a high alert drug because a small error in dose or type can cause severe hypoglycaemia, so a second nurse checks it.

Key Clue: high alert drug needing a double check before administration on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (b) Paracetamol errors are harmful but it is not on the high alert list; (c) Oral iron does not need a double check; (d) Vitamin C is not a high alert drug.

PGI Exam Trap: High alert drugs are treated like any other medicine.

5-Second Recall: Insulin and heparin are high alert drugs.

PNC Exam Pearl: Independent double checks reduce serious medication errors.

question: A staff nurse on the ward is checking how the medicines for a client are stored. Which statement about the storage of medicines is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: Refrigerated medicines are stored with food in the ward fridge
option_2: Medicines are kept at the bedside for convenience
option_3: Left over medicines are kept for the next client
option_4: Medicines are kept in a locked cupboard and checked regularly for expiry dates
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Medicines are kept in a locked cupboard and checked regularly for expiry dates

Clinical Rationale: Medicines are stored in a locked cupboard with regular checks for expiry, so that they stay safe and are NOT taken by anyone else.

Key Clue: storage of medicines on a ward

Priority Principle: Safety / Medication

Why Not Others: (a) Medicines are stored in a separate locked drug fridge; (b) Medicines at the bedside are a danger to children and other clients; (c) Left over medicines may be contaminated or mislabelled.

PGI Exam Trap: Medicines are left at the bedside for easy access.

5-Second Recall: Store medicines locked and check the expiry dates.

PNC Exam Pearl: Return unused medicines to the pharmacy for safe disposal.

question: A 50-year-old man on the ward is prescribed an antacid for indigestion. Which effect is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to expect?
option_1: An increase in the stomach acid
option_2: Neutralisation of the stomach acid
option_3: Delayed emptying of the stomach
option_4: Increased production of bile
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Neutralisation of the stomach acid

Clinical Rationale: An antacid neutralises the acid already present in the stomach and so relieves the burning of indigestion.

Key Clue: effect of a prescribed antacid in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug action

Why Not Others: (a) An antacid lowers rather than raises the stomach acid; (c) Antacids do not delay gastric emptying; (d) Antacids do not increase the production of bile.

PGI Exam Trap: An antacid is thought to increase stomach acid.

5-Second Recall: Antacids neutralise the acid in the stomach.

PNC Exam Pearl: Antacids affect the absorption of many other drugs.

question: A 60-year-old man on the ward is receiving an intravenous drug. Which statement about the care of the intravenous line is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: The dressing is changed only when it falls off
option_2: The same cannula may be left in place for several weeks
option_3: The site is checked for redness, swelling and pain before every dose
option_4: Blood pressure is measured on the arm with the infusion
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) The site is checked for redness, swelling and pain before every dose

Clinical Rationale: Checking the site for redness, swelling and pain before every dose detects phlebitis and infiltration early.

Key Clue: care of an intravenous line in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Safety / Device

Why Not Others: (a) A loose or soiled dressing is replaced at once; (b) A cannula is changed at the recommended interval to prevent infection; (d) Blood pressure on the infused arm disturbs the flow and the site.

PGI Exam Trap: The intravenous site is NOT checked before the dose.

5-Second Recall: Check the cannula site before every dose.

PNC Exam Pearl: Document the site condition and the dressing change.

Reference Table: Normal adult vital signs - Temperature: 36.1-37.2 C (97-99 F); Pulse: 60-100 /min; Respiration: 12-20 /min; Blood pressure: < 120/80 mmHg; SpO2: 95-100% (COPD target 88-92%).

question: A 45-year-old woman on the ward develops an itchy rash with swelling of the face soon after a prescribed drug. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Apply a cold compress and reassure the client
option_2: Give the next dose after an antihistamine
option_3: Record the rash and continue the drug
option_4: Stop the drug, assess the airway and inform the doctor
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Stop the drug, assess the airway and inform the doctor

Clinical Rationale: Facial swelling after a drug can progress to airway obstruction, so the drug is stopped and the airway assessed FIRST.

Key Clue: itchy rash with swelling of the face after a prescribed drug on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) A compress does not treat the swelling airway; (b) An antihistamine does not make a further dose safe; (c) Continuing the drug may lead to a fatal reaction.

PGI Exam Trap: Facial swelling after a drug is treated as a simple rash.

5-Second Recall: Stop the drug and check the airway first.

PNC Exam Pearl: Record the drug as an allergy in the client's notes.

question: A 70-year-old man on the ward has a feeding tube and is prescribed medicines. Which statement about giving the medicines through the tube is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: Give each liquid or crushed medicine separately with a flush of water in between
option_2: Mix all the medicines together in the feeding bag
option_3: Add crushed tablets to the feed and give them as a bolus
option_4: Give enteric coated tablets crushed through the tube
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Give each liquid or crushed medicine separately with a flush of water in between

Clinical Rationale: Each medicine is given separately with a water flush, so that the drugs do NOT interact or block the tube.

Key Clue: giving medicines through a feeding tube in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Skill / Medication

Why Not Others: (b) Mixing medicines can cause interactions and block the tube; (c) Drugs added to the feed may clot the feed and block the tube; (d) Crushing an enteric coated tablet destroys its protective coat.

PGI Exam Trap: All the medicines are mixed together in the feed.

5-Second Recall: Flush the tube before and after each medicine.

PNC Exam Pearl: Use liquid forms where possible instead of crushing tablets.

question: A 40-year-old man on the ward begins to react soon after an intravenous drug is started. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Leave the room to fetch the emergency trolley
option_2: Increase the rate to finish the dose
option_3: Give the rest of the dose slowly
option_4: Stop the infusion at once and keep the line patent
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Stop the infusion at once and keep the line patent

Clinical Rationale: Stopping the infusion at once removes the cause of the reaction while the line is kept open for any emergency drugs.

Key Clue: client reacting soon after an intravenous drug is started on the ward

Priority Principle: Safety / Medication

Why Not Others: (a) Leaving the client alone is unsafe during a reaction; (b) A faster rate gives more of the drug that caused the reaction; (c) Giving the rest of the dose slowly continues the reaction.

PGI Exam Trap: The infusion is continued slowly during a reaction.

5-Second Recall: Stop the infusion first in a suspected drug reaction.

PNC Exam Pearl: Keep the line patent with normal saline for emergency drugs.

question: A mother is measuring a liquid antibiotic for her 3-year-old child at home. Which instruction is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Measure the dose with the spoon or syringe supplied and NOT with a household spoon
option_2: Use a household teaspoon because it is nearly the same
option_3: Give twice the dose if a previous dose was missed
option_4: Give the dose with the child lying flat on the back
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Measure the dose with the spoon or syringe supplied and NOT with a household spoon

Clinical Rationale: Household spoons vary in size and cause wrong doses, so the measuring spoon or oral syringe supplied with the medicine is used.

Key Clue: measuring a liquid antibiotic for a child at home

Priority Principle: Drug calculation

Why Not Others: (b) Household spoons differ widely and cause under or over dosage; (c) Doubling a missed dose can cause harm; (d) Lying flat increases the risk of choking and aspiration.

PGI Exam Trap: A household spoon is used to measure the dose.

5-Second Recall: Use a proper measuring device for liquid medicines.

PNC Exam Pearl: Hold the child upright and give the medicine slowly.

question: A 60-year-old man on the ward is prescribed a drug that strongly reduces stomach acid. Which drug is the MOST likely to be prescribed?
option_1: Ranitidine
option_2: Omeprazole
option_3: Ondansetron
option_4: Domperidone
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Omeprazole

Clinical Rationale: Omeprazole blocks the proton pump in the stomach lining and so strongly reduces the secretion of acid.

Key Clue: drug that strongly reduces stomach acid in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug action

Why Not Others: (a) Ranitidine is an H2 receptor blocker; (c) Ondansetron is an antiemetic; (d) Domperidone is a prokinetic antiemetic.

PGI Exam Trap: The drug groups that reduce acid are confused.

5-Second Recall: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor.

PNC Exam Pearl: Proton pump inhibitors are best taken before breakfast.

question: A 30-year-old man who comes to the clinic is started on treatment for tuberculosis under direct observation. Which statement about directly observed treatment is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: The treatment is stopped as soon as the fever settles
option_2: The client collects a month of tablets and takes them alone
option_3: A health worker watches the client swallow each dose until the course is complete
option_4: The FIRST two weeks of treatment alone need supervision
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) A health worker watches the client swallow each dose until the course is complete

Clinical Rationale: In directly observed treatment a health worker watches the client take every dose, which prevents missed doses and the rise of drug resistance.

Key Clue: directly observed treatment for tuberculosis in a man at the clinic

Priority Principle: Community drug therapy

Why Not Others: (a) Stopping early allows a relapse and drug resistance; (b) Self collection of a month of tablets leads to missed doses; (d) Supervision is needed for the whole course and not only the start.

PGI Exam Trap: Supervision is needed only at the start of the course.

5-Second Recall: Every dose is supervised in directly observed treatment.

PNC Exam Pearl: Missed doses are the main cause of drug resistant tuberculosis.

Reference Table: Normal adult vital signs - Temperature: 36.1-37.2 C (97-99 F); Pulse: 60-100 /min; Respiration: 12-20 /min; Blood pressure: < 120/80 mmHg; SpO2: 95-100% (COPD target 88-92%).

question: A 40-year-old man who comes to the clinic asks about the tablet he has been given in a drug trial. Which statement about the use of a placebo is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: A placebo has no active drug and is used for comparison with the real drug
option_2: A placebo contains a small dose of the active drug
option_3: A placebo is given to the healthy volunteers alone
option_4: A placebo has no place in clinical research
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) A placebo has no active drug and is used for comparison with the real drug

Clinical Rationale: A placebo contains no active drug and is given so that the effect of the real drug can be compared with it.

Key Clue: use of a placebo in a drug trial

Priority Principle: Concept / Pharmacology

Why Not Others: (b) A placebo contains no active drug at all; (c) A placebo is given to control subjects and not only to volunteers; (d) Placebos have an established place in controlled trials.

PGI Exam Trap: A placebo is thought to contain some active drug.

5-Second Recall: A placebo has no active drug and is used as a control.

PNC Exam Pearl: Both groups are treated the same apart from the drug.

question: A 55-year-old man on the ward who is receiving an intravenous heparin infusion develops bleeding gums and blood in the urine. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Increase the infusion rate to keep the line open
option_2: Stop the heparin infusion and inform the doctor at once
option_3: Give vitamin K as prescribed
option_4: Apply pressure to the gums and continue the infusion
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Stop the heparin infusion and inform the doctor at once

Clinical Rationale: Bleeding gums with blood in the urine means the heparin has made the blood too thin, so the infusion is stopped and the doctor informed at once.

Key Clue: bleeding gums and blood in the urine during a heparin infusion in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) A faster rate deepens the bleeding; (c) Vitamin K reverses warfarin and not heparin; (d) Continuing the infusion allows the bleeding to become severe.

PGI Exam Trap: The bleeding is managed by pressure while the heparin continues.

5-Second Recall: Stop heparin at once when bleeding appears.

PNC Exam Pearl: Protamine sulfate is the antidote for heparin.

question: A 40-year-old man who comes to the clinic for epilepsy reports blurred vision and unsteady walking, and his phenytoin level is 28 mcg/mL. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Advise the client to walk more slowly for a few days
option_2: Give the next dose as prescribed
option_3: Withhold the dose and inform the doctor at once
option_4: Double the next dose to reach a steady level
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Withhold the dose and inform the doctor at once

Clinical Rationale: A phenytoin level of 28 micrograms per millilitre is above the therapeutic range and explains the blurred vision and unsteady gait, so the dose is withheld.

Key Clue: blurred vision and unsteady walking with a phenytoin level of 28 mcg/mL

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Advice about walking does not treat the toxic level; (b) Another dose deepens the toxicity; (d) Doubling the dose would be dangerous.

PGI Exam Trap: Signs of toxicity are treated as normal effects of the drug.

5-Second Recall: The therapeutic phenytoin level is 10 to 20 mcg/mL.

PNC Exam Pearl: Blurred vision and ataxia are early signs of phenytoin toxicity.

question: A 45-year-old man on the ward is prescribed subcutaneous insulin. Which order of steps is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to follow?
option_1: Give the insulin and record it at the end of the shift
option_2: Give the injection and then check the blood glucose
option_3: Prepare the dose, check the order and then give it
option_4: Check the order and the client, check the glucose and give the dose
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Check the order and the client, check the glucose and give the dose

Clinical Rationale: The order and the client are checked, the blood glucose is measured, then the dose is prepared and given into the fatty tissue.

Key Clue: order of steps for a subcutaneous insulin injection in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Skill / Medication

Why Not Others: (a) Insulin is recorded at once and not at the end of the shift; (b) The glucose is checked before the dose so that the dose can be adjusted; (c) The order must be checked before the drug is prepared.

PGI Exam Trap: The order is checked after the drug has been prepared.

5-Second Recall: Check the order, the client and the glucose before the insulin.

PNC Exam Pearl: Record the dose, site and time immediately after giving it.

question: A 50-year-old man on the ward is prescribed 500 mg of a drug. The vial contains 1 gram in 4 mL. Which volume is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to draw up?
option_1: 4 mL
option_2: 0.5 mL
option_3: 2 mL
option_4: 8 mL
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) 2 mL

Clinical Rationale: One gram is 1000 milligrams in 4 millilitres, so 500 milligrams needs 2 millilitres of the solution.

Key Clue: prescribed 500 mg from a vial of 1 gram in 4 mL

Priority Principle: Drug calculation

Why Not Others: (a) 4 mL would give the whole gram; (b) 0.5 mL would give only 125 milligrams; (d) 8 mL would give two grams.

PGI Exam Trap: The strength of the vial is read as it stands.

5-Second Recall: Dose needed divided by dose in hand times the volume.

PNC Exam Pearl: Convert grams to milligrams before doing the calculation.

question: A 5-year-old child who weighs 12 kg is prescribed 15 mg/kg of a drug. Which total dose is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: 120 mg
option_2: 180 mg
option_3: 27 mg
option_4: 150 mg
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) 180 mg

Clinical Rationale: Twelve kilograms multiplied by fifteen milligrams per kilogram gives a total dose of one hundred and eighty milligrams.

Key Clue: child weighing 12 kg prescribed 15 mg/kg

Priority Principle: Drug calculation

Why Not Others: (a) 120 milligrams comes from using ten kilograms; (c) 27 milligrams comes from adding the numbers instead of multiplying; (d) 150 milligrams comes from using a different weight.

PGI Exam Trap: The weight and the dose per kilogram are combined wrongly.

5-Second Recall: Multiply the weight in kilograms by the dose per kilogram.

PNC Exam Pearl: Check the maximum daily dose for the child's age.

question: A 65-year-old woman on the ward who takes a diuretic asks about her diet. Which instruction is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Include potassium rich foods such as bananas and greens
option_2: Restrict all the fluids to one litre a day
option_3: Avoid all the fruits and the salt substitutes
option_4: Take the diuretic at bedtime
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Include potassium rich foods such as bananas and greens

Clinical Rationale: Thiazide and loop diuretics lower the potassium, so foods rich in potassium such as bananas and green leafy vegetables are included in the diet.

Key Clue: diet for a woman on the ward taking a prescribed diuretic

Priority Principle: Drug therapy

Why Not Others: (b) Fluid restriction is advised only for a specific reason and not routinely; (c) Fruits are the main source of potassium and are not avoided; (d) A diuretic at bedtime disturbs sleep with frequent urination.

PGI Exam Trap: The potassium loss caused by diuretics is NOT considered.

5-Second Recall: Diuretics can lower the potassium, so advise potassium rich foods.

PNC Exam Pearl: Take diuretics in the morning to avoid night time urination.

question: A 50-year-old man on the ward who is receiving an aminoglycoside antibiotic reports ringing in the ears. Which action is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to take?
option_1: Reassure the client that this is a harmless effect
option_2: Give the next dose and observe the client
option_3: Give a diuretic to protect the ear
option_4: Withhold the drug and inform the doctor at once
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Withhold the drug and inform the doctor at once

Clinical Rationale: Ringing in the ears during an aminoglycoside suggests damage to the hearing, which may become permanent, so the drug is withheld at once.

Key Clue: ringing in the ears during an aminoglycoside antibiotic in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Tinnitus from these drugs is not harmless; (b) Another dose increases the risk of permanent deafness; (c) A diuretic can add to the ear damage.

PGI Exam Trap: A warning sign of ear damage is treated as harmless.

5-Second Recall: Aminoglycosides can damage the ear and the kidney.

PNC Exam Pearl: Watch the kidney function during aminoglycoside therapy.

question: A 25-year-old man on the ward who has just started an antipsychotic develops a stiff neck with the eyes rolling upwards. Which condition is the MOST likely?
option_1: Tardive dyskinesia
option_2: An acute dystonic reaction
option_3: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
option_4: Drug induced parkinsonism
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) An acute dystonic reaction

Clinical Rationale: A stiff neck with the eyes rolling upwards is an acute dystonic reaction, which appears soon after an antipsychotic is started.

Key Clue: stiff neck with the eyes rolling upwards after a new antipsychotic

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Tardive dyskinesia appears late with lip smacking and tongue movements; (c) Neuroleptic malignant syndrome causes fever, rigidity and a rising creatine kinase; (d) Parkinsonism causes tremor, slowness and a mask like face.

PGI Exam Trap: The four drug induced movement disorders are confused.

5-Second Recall: Acute dystonia occurs early and responds to an anticholinergic drug.

PNC Exam Pearl: Note the time of onset to identify the type of reaction.

question: A 60-year-old man on the ward is prescribed 1000 mL of fluid over 8 hours with an infusion pump. Which rate is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to set?
option_1: 125 mL per hour
option_2: 100 mL per hour
option_3: 80 mL per hour
option_4: 250 mL per hour
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) 125 mL per hour

Clinical Rationale: One thousand millilitres divided by eight hours gives one hundred and twenty five millilitres per hour.

Key Clue: 1000 mL over 8 hours with an infusion pump

Priority Principle: Drug calculation

Why Not Others: (b) 100 mL per hour would run for ten hours; (c) 80 mL per hour would run for more than twelve hours; (d) 250 mL per hour would finish in four hours.

PGI Exam Trap: The volume is divided by the wrong time.

5-Second Recall: Divide the total volume by the total hours.

PNC Exam Pearl: Recheck the rate whenever the prescription changes.

question: A 35-year-old woman on the ward who takes an antidepressant in the morning complains of drowsiness during the day. Which action is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to take?
option_1: Tell the client to drink more coffee during the day
option_2: Stop the drug at once without telling the doctor
option_3: Give an extra dose at night
option_4: Ask the doctor about giving the dose in the evening
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Ask the doctor about giving the dose in the evening

Clinical Rationale: Drowsiness during the day may be reduced by moving the dose to the evening, but this change is made only with the doctor's order.

Key Clue: drowsiness during the day on a morning dose of an antidepressant in a woman on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug therapy

Why Not Others: (a) Coffee masks the problem and does not treat it; (b) Stopping the drug suddenly may cause a relapse and withdrawal; (c) An extra dose without an order is unsafe.

PGI Exam Trap: The dose timing is changed without an order.

5-Second Recall: Ask the prescriber before changing the timing of a dose.

PNC Exam Pearl: Many sedating antidepressants are given at night.

question: A 55-year-old man on the ward is prescribed a short acting statin. Which time is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to advise for taking it?
option_1: On waking before breakfast each day
option_2: With the midday meal on MOST days
option_3: In the evening when cholesterol synthesis is highest
option_4: On the days when the cholesterol is high
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) In the evening when cholesterol synthesis is highest

Clinical Rationale: MOST cholesterol is made at night, so a short acting statin taken in the evening works BEST.

Key Clue: timing of a prescribed short acting statin in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug therapy

Why Not Others: (a) The morning is not the ideal time for a short acting statin; (b) The midday meal is not the best time for a short acting statin; (d) A statin is taken daily and not only on some days.

PGI Exam Trap: The drug is taken at the wrong time of day.

5-Second Recall: Short acting statins are best taken at night.

PNC Exam Pearl: Report muscle pain at once as it may mean drug related myopathy.

question: A 60-year-old man on the ward takes several medicines. Which organ is the MOST important in the metabolism of MOST drugs?
option_1: The liver
option_2: The kidney
option_3: The lungs
option_4: The skin
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) The liver

Clinical Rationale: The liver holds the enzyme systems that break down MOST drugs into substances that can be excreted.

Key Clue: organ mainly responsible for drug metabolism in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Clinical physiology

Why Not Others: (b) The kidney excretes drugs and their metabolites; (c) The lungs remove some volatile drugs only; (d) The skin plays a very small part in drug metabolism.

PGI Exam Trap: Metabolism and excretion are confused with each other.

5-Second Recall: The liver metabolises most drugs.

PNC Exam Pearl: Liver disease lengthens the action of many drugs.

question: A 30-year-old man is brought to the clinic drowsy after a suspected drug overdose with a respiratory rate of 8/min. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Wait for the drug screen report before any treatment
option_2: Give a drug to make the client vomit
option_3: Give activated charcoal without checking the airway
option_4: Support the airway and breathing while preparing the prescribed antidote
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Support the airway and breathing while preparing the prescribed antidote

Clinical Rationale: A drowsy client with a respiratory rate of 8 needs the airway and breathing supported FIRST, while the prescribed antidote is prepared.

Key Clue: drowsy client with a respiratory rate of 8/min after a suspected overdose

Priority Principle: ABC / Emergency

Why Not Others: (a) Waiting for the screen delays the life saving treatment; (b) Making the client vomit risks aspiration in a drowsy client; (c) Charcoal is unsafe when the airway is not protected.

PGI Exam Trap: The airway is left unsupported while tests are awaited.

5-Second Recall: Support the airway and breathing first in an overdose.

PNC Exam Pearl: Keep the drug container and any tablets for the doctor to see.

question: A 28-year-old woman who attends the antenatal clinic asks about a medicine that is known to harm the fetus. Which response is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Take the medicine in the third trimester when the fetus is safe
option_2: Take the medicine because small doses are harmless
option_3: Check with the doctor before taking any medicine during pregnancy
option_4: Herbal medicines are safe in pregnancy
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Check with the doctor before taking any medicine during pregnancy

Clinical Rationale: Many drugs cross the placenta, so the client is advised to check with the doctor before taking any medicine during pregnancy.

Key Clue: pregnant woman at the antenatal clinic asking about a medicine that harms the fetus

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) The first trimester is the time of greatest risk of malformation; (b) Even small doses of a harmful drug may damage the fetus; (d) Herbal medicines are not automatically safe in pregnancy.

PGI Exam Trap: A drug that harms the fetus is considered safe in small doses.

5-Second Recall: Check with the doctor before any medicine in pregnancy.

PNC Exam Pearl: The first trimester is the most dangerous time for the fetus.

question: A 30-year-old man who comes to the clinic is prescribed a course of antibiotics. Which advice is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give about completing the course?
option_1: The antibiotic is stopped as soon as the fever settles
option_2: The whole prescribed course is completed even after the client feels better
option_3: The dose may be halved once the client improves
option_4: The antibiotic may be shared with a family member with similar symptoms
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) The whole prescribed course is completed even after the client feels better

Clinical Rationale: The full course is completed so that all the organisms are killed and resistant strains do NOT survive.

Key Clue: completing a prescribed course of antibiotics

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Stopping early allows the infection to return and resistance to develop; (c) Reducing the dose without an order encourages resistance; (d) Sharing antibiotics is unsafe and encourages resistance.

PGI Exam Trap: The course is stopped as soon as the fever settles.

5-Second Recall: Complete the full course of an antibiotic.

PNC Exam Pearl: Finish the course unless the prescriber says otherwise.

question: A 25-year-old woman on the ward is prescribed oral iron. Which side effect is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to tell her about?
option_1: Increased urine output
option_2: A raised blood pressure
option_3: A slow pulse
option_4: Constipation with dark stools
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Constipation with dark stools

Clinical Rationale: Oral iron commonly causes constipation and turns the stool black, which is harmless but often worries clients.

Key Clue: common side effect of prescribed oral iron in a woman on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug action

Why Not Others: (a) Oral iron does not increase the urine output; (b) Oral iron does not raise the blood pressure; (c) Oral iron does not slow the pulse.

PGI Exam Trap: The common bowel effects of iron are NOT mentioned.

5-Second Recall: Iron causes constipation and black stools.

PNC Exam Pearl: Take iron with vitamin C to improve absorption.

question: A 55-year-old man on the ward is prescribed 40 mg of a drug. The stock ampoule contains 100 mg in 2 mL. Which volume is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: 1.6 mL
option_2: 0.4 mL
option_3: 0.8 mL
option_4: 2 mL
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) 0.8 mL

Clinical Rationale: One hundred milligrams are in 2 millilitres, so each millilitre holds 50 milligrams and 40 milligrams need 0.8 millilitre.

Key Clue: prescribed 40 mg from a stock of 100 mg in 2 mL

Priority Principle: Drug calculation

Why Not Others: (a) 1.6 mL would give 80 milligrams; (b) 0.4 mL would give only 20 milligrams; (d) 2 mL would give the whole 100 milligrams.

PGI Exam Trap: The volume is read as if the whole ampoule were the dose.

5-Second Recall: Dose needed over dose in hand times the volume.

PNC Exam Pearl: Have another nurse check the calculation for a high alert drug.

question: A 60-year-old man on the ward is prescribed a beta blocker. Which statement about the action of the drug is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: It raises the heart rate and the blood pressure
option_2: It slows the heart rate and lowers the blood pressure
option_3: It dilates the airways and raises the pulse
option_4: It increases the force of the heart beat
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) It slows the heart rate and lowers the blood pressure

Clinical Rationale: A beta blocker blocks the sympathetic supply to the heart, so the heart rate and the blood pressure both fall.

Key Clue: action of a prescribed beta blocker in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug action

Why Not Others: (a) Beta blockers lower rather than raise the pulse and pressure; (c) Beta blockers can narrow the airways in asthma; (d) Beta blockers reduce rather than increase the force of contraction.

PGI Exam Trap: The action of a beta blocker is reversed.

5-Second Recall: Beta blockers slow the heart and lower the pressure.

PNC Exam Pearl: Watch the pulse before giving a beta blocker.

Reference Table: Normal adult vital signs - Temperature: 36.1-37.2 C (97-99 F); Pulse: 60-100 /min; Respiration: 12-20 /min; Blood pressure: < 120/80 mmHg; SpO2: 95-100% (COPD target 88-92%).

question: A 78-year-old man on the ward is prescribed a drug. Which change is the MOST important in increasing the effect of this drug in the older adult?
option_1: Slower drug metabolism and excretion
option_2: An increased total body water
option_3: A higher basal metabolic rate
option_4: Increased gastric acid secretion
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Slower drug metabolism and excretion

Clinical Rationale: Liver and kidney function fall with age, so drugs are metabolised and excreted more slowly and their effect is prolonged.

Key Clue: factor that increases the effect of a drug in an older adult on the ward

Priority Principle: Clinical physiology

Why Not Others: (b) Body water falls with age and fat rises; (c) The metabolic rate falls rather than rises with age; (d) Gastric acid secretion falls with age.

PGI Exam Trap: Age related changes are ignored when dosing the older client.

5-Second Recall: Start low and go slow in older adults.

PNC Exam Pearl: Falling kidney function prolongs the action of many drugs.

question: A 65-year-old man on the ward is prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin. Which instruction is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Take the tablet with a hot drink
option_2: Swallow the tablet with a glass of water
option_3: Chew the tablet before swallowing it
option_4: Place the tablet under the tongue and let it dissolve
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Place the tablet under the tongue and let it dissolve

Clinical Rationale: The tablet is placed under the tongue where the rich blood supply absorbs it quickly without it passing through the liver.

Key Clue: instruction for sublingual nitroglycerin in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug therapy

Why Not Others: (a) A hot drink does not improve the absorption of the tablet; (b) Swallowing the tablet destroys much of the drug in the liver; (c) Chewing does not give the quick sublingual absorption needed.

PGI Exam Trap: The tablet is swallowed instead of being held under the tongue.

5-Second Recall: Sublingual tablets are kept under the tongue until they dissolve.

PNC Exam Pearl: Sit down before taking nitroglycerin to avoid fainting.

question: A 25-year-old woman in labour on the ward has an oxytocin infusion running, and the monitor shows contractions lasting 90 seconds with little rest between them. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
option_1: Turn the client on to her back and continue the infusion
option_2: Increase the rate to speed up labour
option_3: Stop the oxytocin infusion and inform the doctor
option_4: Record the tracing and continue the infusion as ordered
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) Stop the oxytocin infusion and inform the doctor

Clinical Rationale: Contractions lasting 90 seconds with little rest can reduce the blood supply to the fetus, so the oxytocin is stopped at once and the doctor informed.

Key Clue: contractions lasting 90 seconds with little rest during an oxytocin infusion

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Lying on the back lowers the blood pressure and does not fix the tracing; (b) A faster rate makes the contractions stronger and longer; (d) Continuing the drug allows fetal distress to develop.

PGI Exam Trap: A hyperstimulated uterus is watched while the drug continues.

5-Second Recall: Stop the oxytocin when the contractions are too long or too close.

PNC Exam Pearl: Turn the client on to her left side to improve the fetal blood flow.

question: A 30-year-old mother who visits the clinic asks how to store medicines at home. Which advice is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Keep the medicines in the kitchen near the stove
option_2: Keep the medicines in a locked cupboard out of the reach of children
option_3: Keep the medicines in the child's room for easy use
option_4: Keep the medicines in the bathroom where it stays cool
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Keep the medicines in a locked cupboard out of the reach of children

Clinical Rationale: Medicines kept in a locked cupboard out of reach prevent accidental poisoning of children in the home.

Key Clue: storing medicines at home

Priority Principle: Community drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Heat and moisture near the stove spoil the medicines; (c) Medicines in a child's room invite accidental poisoning; (d) Damp bathrooms spoil medicines and do not keep them safe.

PGI Exam Trap: Medicines are kept where a child can reach them.

5-Second Recall: Store medicines locked and out of the reach of children.

PNC Exam Pearl: Keep the poison control number handy in every home.

question: A 50-year-old man on the ward who takes long term steroids asks about stopping the medicine. Which instruction is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Reduce the dose slowly as prescribed and do NOT stop it suddenly
option_2: Stop the medicine as soon as the symptoms settle
option_3: Double the dose on the days when the symptoms return
option_4: Stop the steroid and start a herbal remedy instead
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Reduce the dose slowly as prescribed and do NOT stop it suddenly

Clinical Rationale: Long term steroids suppress the adrenal glands, so the dose is reduced slowly to allow the glands to recover and avoid an adrenal crisis.

Key Clue: client on long term steroid treatment asking about stopping

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (b) Stopping suddenly can cause a life threatening adrenal crisis; (c) Doubling the dose without an order is unsafe; (d) A herbal remedy does not replace the lost steroid.

PGI Exam Trap: A long term steroid is stopped suddenly.

5-Second Recall: Steroids are tapered and never stopped suddenly.

PNC Exam Pearl: Teach clients to carry a steroid card at all times.

question: A 60-year-old woman on the ward who is taking a prescribed medicine has a raised liver enzyme level on the report. Which action is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to take?
option_1: Double the dose to speed up the effect
option_2: Inform the doctor, as the drug may need to be reviewed
option_3: Stop all the drugs at once without informing anyone
option_4: Ignore the report, as enzymes vary from day to day
solution:
Correct Answer: (b) Inform the doctor, as the drug may need to be reviewed

Clinical Rationale: A raised liver enzyme level may be caused by the drug, so the doctor is informed and the prescription may be reviewed.

Key Clue: raised liver enzyme level in a client taking a prescribed medicine

Priority Principle: Lab interpretation

Why Not Others: (a) A higher dose increases the strain on the liver; (c) Stopping all drugs without advice can cause harm; (d) A raised level is a warning that should not be ignored.

PGI Exam Trap: A useful warning sign on the report is ignored.

5-Second Recall: Report a raised liver enzyme level to the doctor.

PNC Exam Pearl: Ask about nausea, dark urine or jaundice at the same time.

question: A 45-year-old man on the ward has a running infusion and is prescribed an intravenous drug. Which order of steps is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to follow?
option_1: Check the order and the client, clean the port and give the drug
option_2: Give the drug and then check the order
option_3: Clean the port and give the drug without checking the line
option_4: Stop the infusion for good and give the drug through a new line
solution:
Correct Answer: (a) Check the order and the client, clean the port and give the drug

Clinical Rationale: The order and the client are checked, the port cleaned, blood return confirmed and only then is the drug given and the line flushed.

Key Clue: order of steps for an intravenous drug through a running infusion

Priority Principle: Skill / Medication

Why Not Others: (b) The order must always be checked before the drug is given; (c) The line is checked for position and blood return before use; (d) A new line is not needed for every intravenous drug.

PGI Exam Trap: The drug is given before the order and the line are checked.

5-Second Recall: Check the order, the client and the line before every dose.

PNC Exam Pearl: Flush the line with saline between different drugs.

question: A 50-year-old man on the ward is prescribed an oral medicine that irritates the stomach. Which instruction is the MOST appropriate for the nurse to give?
option_1: Take it just before going to bed
option_2: Take it on an empty stomach every time
option_3: Take it together with an antacid
option_4: Take it with food or a glass of milk as advised
solution:
Correct Answer: (d) Take it with food or a glass of milk as advised

Clinical Rationale: A medicine that irritates the stomach is BEST taken with food or milk as advised, which reduces the irritation without spoiling absorption.

Key Clue: oral medicine that irritates the stomach in a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Drug therapy

Why Not Others: (a) Bedtime does not reduce the stomach irritation; (b) An empty stomach increases the irritation; (c) An antacid may bind the drug and reduce its absorption.

PGI Exam Trap: The drug is taken on an empty stomach although it irritates.

5-Second Recall: Give stomach irritating drugs with food or milk.

PNC Exam Pearl: Ask whether the drug should be taken with or without food.

question: A 70-year-old man on the ward is given a medicine with a generic name on the pack. Which statement about the generic name of a drug is the MOST appropriate?
option_1: It changes with each brand of the drug
option_2: It is the name that is given by the maker for advertising
option_3: It is the official non proprietary name and is the same in every country
option_4: It appears on the pack of one particular brand
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) It is the official non proprietary name and is the same in every country

Clinical Rationale: The generic name is the official non proprietary name of the drug and is the same everywhere, unlike the brand names.

Key Clue: generic name of a drug given to a man on the ward

Priority Principle: Concept / Pharmacology

Why Not Others: (a) The generic name does not change with the brand; (b) The maker's own name is the brand name; (d) It is used by every manufacturer and not by one brand.

PGI Exam Trap: The brand name is mistaken for the generic name.

5-Second Recall: The generic name is the same in every country.

PNC Exam Pearl: Prescribe by the generic name to avoid confusion.

question: A 65-year-old man on the ward who takes a prescribed drug develops a persistent dry cough. Which drug is the MOST likely cause?
option_1: A calcium channel blocker given for the pressure
option_2: A beta blocker that is given for the heart
option_3: An angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
option_4: A loop diuretic given for the ankle swelling
solution:
Correct Answer: (c) An angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor

Clinical Rationale: A persistent dry cough is a well known effect of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, caused by the build up of kinins.

Key Clue: persistent dry cough in a man on the ward taking a prescribed drug

Priority Principle: Drug safety

Why Not Others: (a) Calcium channel blockers commonly cause ankle swelling; (b) Beta blockers cause fatigue and cold extremities rather than a cough; (d) Loop diuretics cause a large urine output and low potassium.

PGI Exam Trap: The cough is treated as a chest infection.

5-Second Recall: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors cause a dry cough.

PNC Exam Pearl: The cough settles when the drug is changed to another class.
